claim: 31 bacterial isolates representing four bacterial phyla and 11 genera were selected for genome sequencing using Illumina and PacBio.
source: A total of 31 isolates, representing four bacterial phyla and 11 genera, were selected for genome sequencing using Illumina and PacBio (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of isolates sequenced and the methods used.

claim: 165 bacterial genomes from cheese-associated bacteria were analyzed in total.
source: We also included genomes from the NCBI reference sequence (RefSeq) database that are associated with cheese, for a total of 165 bacterial genomes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of genomes analyzed.

claim: At least one putative horizontally transferred gene was identified in 130 out of 165 (78.8%) cheese-associated species.
source: Based on our most conservative gene identity parameters (minimum 99% identity over 500 nucleotides), we identified at least one putative horizontally transferred gene in 130/165 (78.8%) cheese-associated species in the analysis, for a total of 4733 genes (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers and percentages from the analysis.

claim: 4733 putative horizontally transferred genes were identified in cheese-associated bacteria.
source: Based on our most conservative gene identity parameters (minimum 99% identity over 500 nucleotides), we identified at least one putative horizontally transferred gene in 130/165 (78.8%) cheese-associated species in the analysis, for a total of 4733 genes (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of HGT genes identified.

claim: The 4733 horizontally transferred genes were clustered into 264 individual groups based on genomic proximity.
source: The 4733 genes were clustered into 264 individual groups (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of groups formed from clustering analysis.

claim: Most HGT groups (231, 87.5%) contain only members of the same phylum.
source: Most HGT groups identified (231, 87.5%) contain only members of the same phylum, or even a single genus (183 or 69%, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages from the analysis.

claim: 183 HGT groups (69%) contain only members of a single genus.
source: Most HGT groups identified (231, 87.5%) contain only members of the same phylum, or even a single genus (183 or 69%, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and percentage of single-genus groups.

claim: HGT is most prevalent among closely related species.
source: This supports previous studies which suggest that HGT is most prevalent among closely related species (Ravenhall et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study supporting this claim and presents data consistent with it.

claim: Mobile elements (transposases, conjugal transfer genes, phage-related proteins) represent 13% of all protein coding sequences identified as HGT.
source: Across all of the genes identified in our analysis, the most abundant gene functions are transposases, conjugal transfer genes, phage-related proteins, and other mobile elements (631/4733 or 13% of all protein coding sequences).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages from functional analysis.

claim: 32.6% of all HGT groups contain mobile elements.
source: A third (86/264 or 32.6%) of all HGT groups contain mobile elements.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of groups containing mobile elements.

claim: The most frequent KEGG module among annotated HGT genes is 'metal ion, iron siderophore and vitamin B12 transport systems' (11% of KEGG-annotated genes).
source: Of the KEGG-annotated genes, the most frequent module (281/2264 or 11%) was 'metal ion, iron siderophore and vitamin B12 transport systems'.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages from KEGG annotation analysis.

claim: Five of the 10 largest HGT groups (Groups 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8) contained siderophore transport systems.
source: Five of the 10 largest HGT groups as measured by total number of genes (Groups 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8) contained siderophore transport systems (K02013-K02016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies which groups contain siderophore transport systems.

claim: Low availability of iron in cheese limits the growth of several bacterial species.
source: Low availability of iron in cheese is known to limit the growth of several bacterial species (Monnet et al., 2012, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies demonstrating iron limitation in cheese.

claim: Genes involved in iron acquisition are present in higher numbers in cheese-associated species compared with closely related species from other environments.
source: Previous work has also shown that genes involved in iron acquisition are present in higher numbers in cheese-associated species compared with closely related species from other environments (Monnet et al., 2010; Walter et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing enrichment of iron acquisition genes.

claim: 12% of KEGG-annotated HGT genes are involved in transport of nutrients relevant for growth in the cheese environment.
source: Many other horizontally transferred genes (267/2264 or 12% of KEGG-annotated genes) are also involved in transport of nutrients relevant for growth in the cheese environment.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages from functional analysis.

claim: Lactate is an abundant carbon source in freshly made cheese.
source: Lactate is an abundant carbon source in freshly made cheese, as the initial stages of cheesemaking involve fermentation of lactose to lactate by lactic acid bacteria (Button and Dutton, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing cheese composition and fermentation.

claim: 63 genes (2.8% of KEGG-annotated genes) involved in lactate import were identified as HGT.
source: We observed a large number of genes (63/2264 or 2.8% of KEGG-annotated genes) involved in lactate import (lactate permease - K03303) or lactate metabolism.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages from functional analysis.

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase represented nearly 1% of all horizontally transferred protein coding sequences.
source: Lactate dehydrogenase (K00101), which reduces lactate to pyruvate, represented nearly 1% of all horizontally transferred protein coding sequences.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage from functional analysis.

claim: The primary source of energy for microbial growth in cheese is metabolism of abundant lipids and proteins, particularly casein.
source: Apart from lactate, the primary source of energy for microbial growth in cheese is metabolism of the abundant lipids and proteins, particularly casein (Monnet et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing cheese composition and microbial metabolism.

claim: Less than 1% of KEGG-annotated HGT genes are related to drug resistance.
source: However, less than 1% of KEGG-annotated genes in this dataset are related to drug resistance.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage from functional analysis.

claim: A tetracycline resistance gene was identified in eight Brevibacterium species (group 10).
source: A tetracycline resistance gene was identified in eight Brevibacterium species (group 10) and a tripartite multidrug resistance system (K03446, K03543) in three Pseudomonas species (group 37).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies specific antibiotic resistance genes and their distribution.

claim: A tripartite multidrug resistance system was identified in three Pseudomonas species (group 37).
source: A tetracycline resistance gene was identified in eight Brevibacterium species (group 10) and a tripartite multidrug resistance system (K03446, K03543) in three Pseudomonas species (group 37).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies specific antibiotic resistance genes and their distribution.

claim: Group 1 (ActinoRUSTI) is the largest HGT region identified in cheese-associated bacteria, spanning approximately 47 kbp and containing 34 genes.
source: The largest HGT region we identified in cheese-associated bacteria, Group 1, includes an island of ~47 kbp (~1% of the genome of B. linens JB5) and 34 genes.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific size measurements and gene counts.

claim: Group 1 (ActinoRUSTI) is found in whole or in part in 15 different species across five Actinobacterial genera and one Firmicute.
source: This island is found in whole or in part in 15 different species in five different Actinobacterial genera (Brachybacterium, Brevibacterium, Corynebacterium, Microbacterium, and Glutamicibacter, formerly Arthrobacter), and one Firmicute (Alkalibacterium).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists the species and genera containing this HGT region.

claim: The core of ActinoRUSTI contains genes predicted to form a siderophore import complex, including substrate binding proteins, membrane permeases, and an ATPase subunit.
source: The core of this region, flanked by AraC-like transcriptional regulators (e.g. Ga0099663_102740 and Ga0099663_102753 from JB182), contains several genes predicted to form a siderophore import complex, including two cell-surface associated substrate binding protein genes (Ga0099663_102743–44), two membrane permease genes (Ga0099663_102745–46), and an ATPase subunit (Ga0099663_102747).
evidence: The manuscript describes the gene content based on annotation and prediction.

claim: RUSTI genes in G. arilaitensis JB182 were significantly upregulated in the presence of Penicillium compared to growth alone.
source: The genes in RUSTI were significantly upregulated in the presence of a competing microbe relative to growth alone (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1f), suggesting that this horizontally transferred region is transcriptionally active and may be responding to competition for limited iron in cheese.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression.

claim: The upregulation of RUSTI genes in the presence of competition suggests this horizontally transferred region is transcriptionally active and may be responding to competition for limited iron in cheese.
source: The genes in RUSTI were significantly upregulated in the presence of a competing microbe relative to growth alone (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1f), suggesting that this horizontally transferred region is transcriptionally active and may be responding to competition for limited iron in cheese.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the RNA-seq data in the context of iron competition.

claim: The RUSTI permease subunits and ATP binding subunit share substantial homology with the catechol ferric enterobactin transport system (FepD, FepG, and FepC) in E. coli.
source: The two genes annotated as permease subunits and one gene annotated as an ATP binding subunit each share substantial homology with the catechol ferric enterobactin transport system (FepD, FepG, and FepC, respectively) in E. coli (Elkins and Earhart, 1989; Shea and McIntosh, 1991; Chenault and Earhart, 1991).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from BLAST comparison to TCDB database.

claim: Group 7 (ProteoRUSTI) is found in several Vibrio and Halomonas species and contains an ABC siderophore transport system.
source: The HGT group with the most protein coding genes that we identified in γ-Proteobacteria (Group 7) is found in several Vibrio and Halomonas species, and like ActinoRUSTI contains an ABC siderophore transport system with individual substrate-binding, permease, and ATP-binding domains (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the gene content and distribution of this HGT group.

claim: ProteoRUSTI (Group 7) appears to have analogous function to ActinoRUSTI in iron acquisition but does not appear to be related.
source: Although this group appears to have analogous function in the acquisition of iron with RUSTI from Actinobacteria, this ProteoRUSTI does not appear to be related.
evidence: The manuscript compares the two HGT regions and concludes they are functionally analogous but not homologous.

claim: Group 7 (ProteoRUSTI) also contains genes related to the Phn family involved in phosphonate import and metabolism.
source: The same gene island also contains genes related to the Phn family involved in phosphonate import and metabolism (Jochimsen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript describes additional gene content in this HGT region with citation.

claim: Phosphonate metabolism genes have previously been associated with iron siderophore acquisition in acidic environments.
source: Phosphonate metabolism genes have previously been associated with iron siderophore acquisition in acidic environments (Osorio et al., 2008), and cheese is typically close to pH5 during the initial periods of rind community growth.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study linking phosphonate metabolism to iron acquisition.

claim: Cheese is typically close to pH5 during the initial periods of rind community growth.
source: Phosphonate metabolism genes have previously been associated with iron siderophore acquisition in acidic environments (Osorio et al., 2008), and cheese is typically close to pH5 during the initial periods of rind community growth.
evidence: The manuscript states a fact about cheese pH.

claim: Several uropathogenic E. coli strains share identical DNA sequences with the ProteoRUSTI region.
source: Interestingly, BLAST of this region against the NCBI RefSeq database reveals that several uropathogenic E. coli strains share identical DNA sequences (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from BLAST searches against NCBI database.

claim: Iron sequestration by animals is a common defense against pathogens.
source: Iron sequestration by animals is a common defense against pathogens (Parrow et al., 2013), and enhanced iron acquisition is commonly associated with virulence.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference about host defense mechanisms.

claim: Enhanced iron acquisition is commonly associated with virulence.
source: Iron sequestration by animals is a common defense against pathogens (Parrow et al., 2013), and enhanced iron acquisition is commonly associated with virulence.
evidence: The manuscript states a general principle about pathogen virulence.

claim: Mammals produce lactoferrin in milk for iron sequestration.
source: Mammals produce lactoferrin in milk for the same reason (Ellison, 1994), and these data suggest that the same genes would be adaptive in both pathogenesis and growth on cheese.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference about lactoferrin function in milk.

claim: Two species of cheese-associated Staphylococcus (S. fleuretti CIP106114 and S. vitulinus Ma1) share a large (~20 kb) cluster of genes (Group 31) that includes hemolysin and fibronectin binding protein.
source: Two species of cheese-associated Staphylococcus (S. fleuretti CIP106114 and S. vitulinus Ma1) share a large (~20 kb) cluster of genes (Group 31) that includes hemolysin and fibronectin binding protein (FnBP), which are involved in virulence in S. aureus (Sinha et al., 1999; Cheung and Ying, 1994).
evidence: The manuscript describes the gene content of this HGT group with citations.

claim: Hemolysin and fibronectin binding protein are involved in virulence in S. aureus.
source: Two species of cheese-associated Staphylococcus (S. fleuretti CIP106114 and S. vitulinus Ma1) share a large (~20 kb) cluster of genes (Group 31) that includes hemolysin and fibronectin binding protein (FnBP), which are involved in virulence in S. aureus (Sinha et al., 1999; Cheung and Ying, 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites references about virulence factors in S. aureus.

claim: FnBP has been implicated in formation of biofilms in methicillin resistant S. aureus.
source: FnBP enables binding to and invasion of cells, and has been implicated in formation of biofilms in methicillin resistant S. aureus (McCourt et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference about FnBP function.

claim: Group 31 contains genes for iron acquisition that are homologous to the EfeUOB systems in E. coli and Bacillus subtilis and FepABC system in S. aureus, which are active in low-pH conditions.
source: Group 31 also contains genes for iron acquisition. These genes are homologous to the EfeUOB systems in E. coli and Bacillus subtilis and FepABC system in S. aureus, which are active in low-pH conditions (Cao et al., 2007; Miethke et al., 2013; Turlin et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes gene homology with citations about function.

claim: ActinoRUSTI gene islands at least 97% identical were identified in 23 (61%) of 38 cheese metagenomes analyzed.
source: Gene islands at least 97% identical to ActinoRUSTI were readily identified in 23 (61%) of these metagenomes, in both natural and washed rind cheeses from the United States and Europe.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from metagenomic BLAST searches.

claim: ProteoRUSTI was identified in 26% of the 38 cheese metagenomes analyzed.
source: Although less common (26% of metagenomes), ProteoRUSTI was also identified in diverse cheeses in both the US and Europe.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from metagenomic BLAST searches.

claim: StaphRUSTI could not be found in any of the 38 metagenomes analyzed.
source: StaphRUSTI could not be found in any of the metagenomes we analyzed.
evidence: The manuscript reports negative results from metagenomic BLAST searches.

claim: Siderophore-associated HGT islands are widespread in cheese rind microbiomes.
source: These data demonstrate that siderophore-associated HGT islands are widespread in cheese rind microbiomes.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the metagenomic analysis data.

claim: The Glutamicibacter JB182 RUSTI region contains a recombinase of the site-specific tyrosine recombinase XerD family.
source: Analysis of the Glutamicibacter JB182 RUSTI region revealed homologs of each of these protein classes (Figure 3A): a recombinase of the site-specific tyrosine recombinase XerD family (Ga0099663_102762) (Subramanya et al., 1997), a hexameric ATPase conjugation protein of the VirD4/TraG/TraD family (Ga0099663_102784) (Hamilton et al., 2000), and a homolog of the bi-functional primase-polymerase DNA replication protein family (Ga0099663_102766).
evidence: The manuscript reports identification of specific protein homologs with citations.

claim: The Glutamicibacter JB182 RUSTI region contains a hexameric ATPase conjugation protein of the VirD4/TraG/TraD family.
source: Analysis of the Glutamicibacter JB182 RUSTI region revealed homologs of each of these protein classes (Figure 3A): a recombinase of the site-specific tyrosine recombinase XerD family (Ga0099663_102762) (Subramanya et al., 1997), a hexameric ATPase conjugation protein of the VirD4/TraG/TraD family (Ga0099663_102784) (Hamilton et al., 2000), and a homolog of the bi-functional primase-polymerase DNA replication protein family (Ga0099663_102766).
evidence: The manuscript reports identification of specific protein homologs with citations.

claim: The Glutamicibacter JB182 RUSTI region contains a homolog of the bi-functional primase-polymerase DNA replication protein family.
source: Analysis of the Glutamicibacter JB182 RUSTI region revealed homologs of each of these protein classes (Figure 3A): a recombinase of the site-specific tyrosine recombinase XerD family (Ga0099663_102762) (Subramanya et al., 1997), a hexameric ATPase conjugation protein of the VirD4/TraG/TraD family (Ga0099663_102784) (Hamilton et al., 2000), and a homolog of the bi-functional primase-polymerase DNA replication protein family (Ga0099663_102766).
evidence: The manuscript reports identification of specific protein homologs.

claim: Actinobacterial ICE systems typically use conjugation apparatus belonging to the SpoIIE/FtsK family, which allows transfer of double-stranded DNA.
source: Interestingly, Actinobacterial ICE systems typically use conjugation apparatus belonging to the SpoIIE/FtsK family, which allows transfer of double-stranded DNA (te Poele et al., 2008; Bordeleau et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites references about typical Actinobacterial ICE systems.

claim: The conjugation machinery in ActinoRUSTI is more reminiscent of gram-negative and Firmicute systems of single-stranded transfer.
source: However, the conjugation machinery here is more reminiscent of gram-negative and Firmicute systems of single-stranded transfer (Burrus and Waldor, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript compares the conjugation machinery to other systems with citation.

claim: ICE integration frequently occurs at the 3' end of tRNA genes.
source: ICE integration is site-specific, and frequently occurs at the 3' end of tRNA genes (Ghinet et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference about ICE integration sites.

claim: A leucine tRNA is located immediately downstream of the RUSTI region in Glutamicibacter.
source: Immediately downstream of the RUSTI region in Glutamicibacter is a leucine tRNA.
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic context of RUSTI.

claim: The 3' end of the tRNA-Leu forms an imperfect repeat with the region immediately upstream of the RUSTI region, suggesting it is used as the integration site.
source: The 3' end of the tRNA forms an imperfect repeat with the region immediately upstream of the RUSTI region, which strongly suggests that the tRNA-Leu is used at the integration site (att site) for this ICE.
evidence: The manuscript describes sequence analysis suggesting the integration site.

claim: PCR products suggest that at least a portion of G. arilaitensis JB182 cells have lost the RUSTI ICE from their chromosome and it is present as an extrachromosomal circular form.
source: We were able to detect PCR products which suggest that at least a portion of the cells within the population have lost the RUSTI ICE from their chromosome, and it is present as an extrachromosomal circular form (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports PCR results indicating ICE excision.

claim: Sequencing of the PCR product spanning the predicted excision site matched the predicted remaining sequence, containing Repeat element B.
source: Sequencing of the PCR product (primers 1 + 6) that spans the predicted excision site matched the predicted remaining sequence, containing Repeat element B (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports DNA sequencing results confirming the excision site.

claim: Sequencing of the PCR product spanning the predicted circularization site matched the predicted sequence, containing Repeat element A.
source: Sequencing of the PCR product (primers 2 + 5) that spans the predicted circularization site matched the predicted sequence, containing Repeat element A (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript reports DNA sequencing results confirming the circular form.

claim: ActinoRUSTI was positively identified in one of five common starter cultures tested by PCR.
source: We tested five common starter cultures for the presence of ActinoRUSTI by PCR, and positively identified it in one of these (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports PCR results from testing starter cultures.

claim: The starter culture containing ActinoRUSTI is known to contain Brevibacterium linens and Glutamicibacter nicotinae.
source: This culture is known to contain two species of Actinobacteria, Brevibacterium linens and Glutamicibacter nicotinae.
evidence: The manuscript states the known composition of the starter culture.

claim: One Brevibacterium isolate from the starter culture tested positive for ActinoRUSTI by PCR.
source: SSU sequencing revealed that two isolates were Glutamicibacter and two were Brevibacterium. One of the Brevibacterium isolates tested positive for ActinoRUSTI by PCR (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports PCR and sequencing results from isolates.

claim: HGT has been previously documented in cheese-associated Penicillium species.
source: Indeed, HGT has been previously documented in cheese-associated Penicillium species (Cheeseman et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on fungal HGT in cheese.

claim: Bacterial-fungal gene transfer has been documented in other environments, although it is thought to be rare.
source: HGT between bacteria and fungi has also been documented in other environments, although it is thought to be rare (Keeling and Palmer, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference about bacterial-fungal HGT.

claim: The method for identifying HGT does not permit determination of the direction of gene flow.
source: Our method for identifying HGT does not permit determination of the direction of gene flow, and indeed it seems likely that the original sources of many of these genetic elements are not present in our dataset.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states a limitation of the method.

claim: Iron is limiting for Glutamicibacter, Brevibacterium, and Corynebacterium species growing on cheese.
source: Although previous studies demonstrated that iron is limiting for Glutamicibacter, Brevibacterium, and Corynebacterium species growing on cheese (Monnet et al., 2012, 2010), the preponderance of siderophore and other iron acquisition genes we observed being horizontally transferred suggests that the same is true across bacterial phyla.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies demonstrating iron limitation.

claim: The preponderance of siderophore and other iron acquisition genes being horizontally transferred suggests that iron is limiting across bacterial phyla in cheese.
source: Although previous studies demonstrated that iron is limiting for Glutamicibacter, Brevibacterium, and Corynebacterium species growing on cheese (Monnet et al., 2012, 2010), the preponderance of siderophore and other iron acquisition genes we observed being horizontally transferred suggests that the same is true across bacterial phyla.
evidence: The manuscript infers broader iron limitation from the HGT data.

claim: Limiting iron is a deliberate strategy on the part of mammalian hosts to block the growth of infectious microbes.
source: Limiting iron is a deliberate strategy on the part of mammalian hosts to block the growth of infectious microbes, and this strategy influences the composition of milk because of the presence of lactoferrin (Ellison, 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference about host defense mechanisms.

claim: Convergent strategies for acquiring iron are used by pathogens and by cheese-associated microbes.
source: Interestingly, convergent strategies for acquiring iron are used by pathogens and by cheese-associated microbes and we observe that in some cases these disparate species appear to have shared genes through horizontal transfer.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the comparative analysis of HGT genes.

claim: In some cases, pathogens and cheese-associated microbes appear to have shared iron acquisition genes through horizontal transfer.
source: Interestingly, convergent strategies for acquiring iron are used by pathogens and by cheese-associated microbes and we observe that in some cases these disparate species appear to have shared genes through horizontal transfer.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from sequence comparisons.

claim: The presence of iron acquisition genes in ocean-dwelling microbes suggests these genes have broad utility for the common challenge of iron limitation.
source: The presence of these same genes in a microbe found in ocean habitats suggests that these genes have broad utility for the common challenge of iron limitation.
evidence: The manuscript infers broad utility from the distribution of genes across environments.

claim: ActinoRUSTI genes are upregulated in response to other species.
source: Given that iron is limiting in cheese, and that ActinoRUSTI genes are upregulated in response to other species (Figure 4C), it is likely that these genes are functional and may play a role in competition.
evidence: The manuscript refers to RNA-seq data showing upregulation.

claim: It is likely that ActinoRUSTI genes are functional and may play a role in competition.
source: Given that iron is limiting in cheese, and that ActinoRUSTI genes are upregulated in response to other species (Figure 4C), it is likely that these genes are functional and may play a role in competition.
evidence: The manuscript infers function from expression data and environmental context.

claim: The prevalence of siderophore import, but not siderophore synthesis pathways suggests that species may cheat by scavenging the biosynthetic products of others.
source: The prevalence of siderophore import, but not siderophore synthesis pathways suggests that species may cheat by scavenging the biosynthetic products of others (Cordero et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript infers a cheating strategy from the gene content with citation.

claim: The possibility that a starter culture is the source of mobile gene elements suggests that genomic content, rather than just specific species, must be considered when designing microbial supplements.
source: In particular, the possibility that a starter culture is the source of mobile gene elements suggests that the genomic content, rather than just specific species, must be considered when designing microbial supplements.
evidence: The manuscript draws an implication from the starter culture findings.

claim: The need to screen for clinically relevant elements such as antibiotic resistance genes in probiotics is widely recognized.
source: The need to screen for clinically relevant elements such as antibiotic resistance genes is widely recognized (Sanders et al., 2010), but other mobile gene elements from these organisms may also enter native microbial populations with unknown consequences.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference about screening requirements for probiotics.

claim: Other mobile gene elements from probiotic organisms may enter native microbial populations with unknown consequences.
source: The need to screen for clinically relevant elements such as antibiotic resistance genes is widely recognized (Sanders et al., 2010), but other mobile gene elements from these organisms may also enter native microbial populations with unknown consequences.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about potential consequences of mobile elements.

claim: Cheese rind-associated bacteria are readily isolated and cultured.
source: By contrast, cheese rind-associated bacteria are readily isolated and cultured, and model communities may enable identification of features of microbial communities and their environments that alter frequency and extent of HGT.
evidence: The manuscript states a characteristic of the cheese rind system.

claim: Model cheese rind communities may enable identification of features that alter frequency and extent of HGT.
source: By contrast, cheese rind-associated bacteria are readily isolated and cultured, and model communities may enable identification of features of microbial communities and their environments that alter frequency and extent of HGT.

source: The in vitro cheese system enables experimental manipulation to investigate the role of community composition in driving HGT.

source: Using cheese rinds as a model system could help elucidate the factors that influence the frequency of HGT, how it impacts competition and cooperation, and helps shape a microbiome.
evidence: The manuscript proposes potential applications of the model system.

source: Comparing 31 newly sequenced and 134 previously sequenced bacterial isolates from cheese rinds, we identified over 200 putative horizontally transferred genomic regions containing 4733 protein coding genes.

source: The largest of these regions are enriched for genes involved in siderophore acquisition, and are widely distributed in cheese rinds in both Europe and the US.

claim: Identification of genes that are frequently transferred in a particular environment may provide insight into the selective forces shaping microbial communities.
source: These results suggest that HGT is prevalent in cheese rind microbiomes, and that identification of genes that are frequently transferred in a particular environment may provide insight into the selective forces shaping microbial communities.
evidence: The abstract proposes a general principle from the findings.

claim: HGT is a major force in microbial evolution and can lead to the wholesale acquisition of novel functions.
source: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major force in microbial evolution and can lead to the wholesale acquisition of novel functions.
evidence: The manuscript states a general principle about HGT.

source: In some cases, these novel functions can have significant adaptive consequences, such as in the transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (Ochman et al., 2000).

source: HGT also allows rapid adaptation to new niches (Wiedenbeck and Cohan, 2011), as ecologically relevant genes may be acquired by species not previously adapted to a particular niche (Tasse et al., 2010; Hehemann et al., 2010).
